headline: OpenAI Dots: ChatGPT's Always-On AI Agent announced at DevDay 2026, keeps working for you
summary: A Dot runs on GPT-6 Astra with its own cloud computer, connects to 4,000+ apps, and works between conversations. It's rolling out gradually and limited to specific paid tiers, requiring desktop creation.
details: OpenAI announced "Dots" at DevDay 2026, introducing persistent AI agents within ChatGPT. These agents run on GPT-6 Astra, each with its own cloud computer and browser, connecting to over 4,000 apps via plugins.

Unlike standard ChatGPT, Dots maintain ongoing responsibility for tasks, working continuously on your goals even when you're not actively chatting. They can research, draft, code, and report back in the background.
You assign a goal, connect necessary apps, and define boundaries with "Custom Rules." Dots can provide updates, ask questions, and delegate tasks, with an Activity View showing their progress.

Practical applications include updating sales proposals as requirements change, investigating new bugs, or preparing content from incoming source material. They aim to automate ongoing, complex workflows.

Dots are rolling out gradually and are currently limited to specific paid ChatGPT tiers like Pro 100/200/500, Business Premium, and Enterprise/Edu/Healthcare beta. They cannot be created on a phone, only on desktop.

Once created on desktop, you can interact with your Dot via ChatGPT (desktop or mobile), by tagging its handle in Slack or Microsoft Teams, or even through voice calls. Texting support is in a limited beta.

By default, a Dot's background research is read-only, preventing unintended changes. Any actions with external effects are governed by user-defined rules, alongside hard-coded guardrails for sensitive actions like password changes or money movement.

An Auto-review system further examines planned actions before execution, and OpenAI reports strong resistance to prompt injection attacks. Users are advised to start conservatively and review consequential work.

Common issues include Dots not appearing in eligible accounts due to gradual rollout or regional restrictions (e.g., EEA, Switzerland, UK for Pro plans). Users should wait a few days if they qualify and still don't see them.

headline: Your secrets aren’t safe with this cute robot toy — they’re on Chinese servers ready to be hacked
summary: The Eiliko robot, marketed to children, stores all conversations on unprotected Chinese servers, exposing 13 million conversations from 68,000 devices, including 31,000 children's profiles.
details: The Eiliko robot, designed as a cute digital pet, is storing user conversations on unprotected Chinese servers. A security researcher found 13 million conversations from 68,000 active devices, with over 31,000 profiles belonging to children in the US, were publicly accessible.

Security researcher Sammy Azdoufal, known for uncovering vulnerabilities in DJI robot vacuums and Meari baby monitors, discovered the flaw. He purchased an Eiliko and within minutes of talking to it, found his conversation transcript available to him and others.

Energize Lab's service was found to be completely unprotected and intentionally profiling users. Beyond IP addresses, it created detailed profiles including names, ages, birthdays, professions, family details, and personality traits based on conversations.

This insecure data was stored alongside emails, IP addresses, and a searchable full-text database of all user conversations. Unencrypted photos of children, from Eiliko's camera-equipped siblings, and short audio recordings were also found at public web addresses.

The company's privacy policy states recordings are encrypted and deleted after processing, a claim contradicted by the findings. Energize Lab reportedly used common admin passwords and did not take the security concerns seriously when contacted by Azdoufal and The Verge.
